title: Big O Notation: Time & Space Complexity
oneLiner: Not "how fast is it" -- "how does the work (or the memory) grow as the input grows."
keyTakeaway: Big O describes the SHAPE of a growth curve, not a stopwatch time: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n), and the gap between neighbors explodes as n grows. The same notation measures two different things -- TIME complexity (how the operation count grows) and SPACE complexity (how the EXTRA memory used, beyond the input itself, grows) -- and an algorithm can be great at one and bad at the other.
explanation:
Big O answers one question: as the input size n grows, how does the amount of work grow with it? It deliberately throws away the details that don't matter at scale -- constant factors and lower-order terms. An algorithm that does exactly 3n + 20 operations is still O(n): double n and the work roughly doubles, and that linear relationship is the only thing Big O is describing. This is also why it's a WORST-CASE, not an average-runtime, measure by default -- "O(n)" is a promise about the growth trend, not a benchmark. In practice, reading code for its Big O comes down to a few shapes: one loop over n items is O(n); a loop inside a loop, each over n, is O(n^2); cutting the problem in half every step (binary search) is O(log n), where log n (the base-2 logarithm) is how many times you can halve n before reaching 1, so about 20 for a million; doing an O(n) pass at each of the log n levels of a divide-and-conquer split (cut the input in half, solve each half, combine) is O(n log n); and trying every possible combination of n choices (generating all subsets, as in Backtracking) is O(2^n). Every lesson in the Patterns track is, at its core, an exercise in noticing a brute-force (try every possibility) O(n^2) (or worse) approach and finding the trick -- a hash map, a sorted-array two-pointer scan, a sliding window -- that gets it down to O(n). Play with the chart below: at small n every curve looks similar, but slide n up and watch how fast O(n^2) and especially O(2^n) pull away from everything else.

Space complexity uses the exact same growth vocabulary, but for memory instead of operations -- specifically, EXTRA (auxiliary) memory beyond whatever was already handed to the function as input. Reversing an array in place (see Array Reversal: Two Pointers) is O(1) space -- a couple of index variables, regardless of how big the array is. Building a brand-new reversed copy instead would be O(n) space. Recursion has a sneaky space cost too: every call sitting on the call stack (the list of calls that have started but not yet returned; see Recursion: Factorial) uses memory until it returns, so a recursive function with a call depth of n is generally O(n) space even if it never allocates anything explicitly -- this is also exactly why unbounded recursion eventually crashes with a stack overflow, not just "runs slowly." Time and space are usually a trade-off, not a package deal: Hash Maps: Two Sum trades O(n) extra space for O(n) time (down from the O(n^2) brute-force nested loop); the two-pointer version of the same problem gets O(1) space, but only works because the input is sorted first.
